messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Kiet's eyes would glaze over as he tried to recount the events of that fateful night three years ago. He was a journalist, known for his fearless pursuit of truth, but the memories of his torture at the hands of government officials still felt like a distant dream. The sounds of children crying echoed in his mind, transporting him back to the dimly lit room where he was held captive. It was as if the cries were seared into his brain, and even now, whenever he heard kids wailing, he would feel an overwhelming sense of dread. As a journalist, Kiet's work often took him to crowded areas, but since the incident, he had become increasingly withdrawn. He avoided social gatherings, fearing that people who knew him before the event would see right through him, sensing the shame and guilt that he carried. His friends and family tried to reach out, but Kiet pushed them away, feeling defective and unworthy of their love. Even simple tasks like eating became a chore. Kiet would often restrict his food intake as a way of coping with the emotions that threatened to overwhelm him. He believed that if he could just control something, anything, he might be able to ward off the feelings of powerlessness that lingered long after his release. His colleagues at the newspaper noticed his weight loss and expressed concern, but Kiet brushed it off, too ashamed to reveal the truth. The memories of his torture were fragmented, like pieces of a puzzle that refused to fit together. When he tried to deliberately recall what happened, Kiet found himself hitting a wall. The events felt unreal, as if they had occurred to someone else. He would get glimpses of images - a chair, a table, a pair of hands - but the details remained elusive. There were moments when he wondered if it had all been just a terrible dream. Kiet's days were filled with rumination, his mind consumed by thoughts of how the event could have been prevented. If only he had taken a different route that night, if only he had kept a lower profile, maybe things would be different now. He became hyper-vigilant, constantly watching others for signs of potential harm. The sound of footsteps behind him made him jump; the rustling of papers sounded like whispers in his ear. As a journalist, Kiet was no stranger to danger, but this was different. This was personal. He felt exposed, as if others could see right through him, sense the shame and guilt that he carried. His values had been violated, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was somehow to blame for what happened. Lately, Kiet's editor had noticed a decline in his work quality. His stories lacked depth, and his sources seemed reluctant to talk to him. It was as if Kiet's inability to recall the events of that night had seeped into every aspect of his life. He knew he needed help, but the thought of reliving those memories terrified him. As Kiet sat in his small apartment, surrounded by the echoes of a life left unlived, he realized that he couldn't keep running. The sounds of children crying still lingered in his mind, a constant reminder of what he had endured. He knew it was time to face his demons head-on, no matter how painful it might be. With a sense of trepidation, Kiet picked up the phone and dialed the number of a therapist, hoping that she could help him unravel the tangled threads of his memory and find some semblance of peace.
